Adding a New Task Type

Sebastian Fischer

Source: vignettes/articles/new_task_type.Rmd
new_task_type.Rmd

The Custom Learning Problems article shows how to use the generic TaskTorch for learning problems beyond classification and regression. This is the best approach for one-off modeling problems that are not supported out of the box by {mlr3torch}. If you instead want to create a task type that is fully integrated into the {mlr3} ecosystem, e.g. for creating an extension package, this article will show you how to do that. If you want to do so, it is best to get in touch with us to discuss the implementation and provide guidance.

As a running example, we use a very simple task type "count" for count data, i.e., Poisson regression. Note that we are showing a minimal implementation for illustrative purposes that omits some input checks to keep the example concise.

library(mlr3torch)
#> Loading required package: mlr3
#> Loading required package: mlr3pipelines
#> Loading required package: torch
library(data.table)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'data.table'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     %notin%
library(R6)

Registering the Task Type with mlr3

A task type in {mlr3} consists of a Task, a Prediction and a Measure class (and a Learner, which we cover afterwards), which have to be registered in mlr_reflections. mlr_reflections is the central registry of {mlr3}: an environment with lookup tables that define what is valid for each task type, e.g., the class names, the column roles, the properties, and the predict types. All of its entries are documented in mlr_reflections. Instead of hard-coding the task types, {mlr3} looks them up in these tables, so registering a new task type there makes it available throughout {mlr3}. These are independent of {mlr3torch} and required for any new task type in {mlr3}, so we keep them as short as possible here. If the task type is already defined by another package, e.g. survival tasks in {mlr3survival}, you can skip this section and continue with Supporting the Task Type in mlr3torch. For more information, always consult the documentation of the classes we inherit from, such as ?mlr3::TaskSupervised, ?mlr3::Prediction, ?mlr3::Measure, and ?mlr3torch::LearnerTorch. For our count task, the target is a single integer column and we are inheriting from TaskSupervised because it is a supervised learning problem.

TaskCount = R6Class("TaskCount", inherit = TaskSupervised,
  public = list(
    initialize = function(id, backend, target, label = NA_character_) {
      super$initialize(id = id, task_type = "count", backend = backend, target = target,
        label = label)
    },
    truth = function(rows = NULL) super$truth(rows)[[1L]]
  )
)

The only property we need to check for the task’s metadata is that the target is a single integer column. We do this by implementing task_check_col_roles.TaskCount():

task_check_col_roles.TaskCount = function(task, new_roles, ...) {
  target = new_roles$target
  if (length(target) > 1L) {
    stop("Count tasks must have exactly one target column")
  }
  if (length(target) && task$col_info[list(target), "type", on = "id"][[1L]] != "integer") {
    stop(sprintf("Target column '%s' must be an integer column", target))
  }
  NextMethod()
}

Next, we define the structure of the prediction objects for this task type. A prediction for this task type contains the predicted rate as the response, i.e., the expected count, which is the parameter \(\lambda\) of the Poisson distribution. For simplicity, we only support this single predict type "response", but a task type can have multiple predict types, e.g., "response" and "se" for regression.

Internally, {mlr3} mostly works with a lightweight representation of predictions: an S3 object of class PredictionData<Type>, i.e., a named list with class c("PredictionDataCount", "PredictionData"). It is also what is stored in the user-facing Prediction object, which is an R6 class and is returned, e.g., by learner$predict(). Note that the $response() method needs to handle a non-existing target column to support prediction in the inference setting where no ground truth is available.

new_prediction_data_count = function(row_ids, truth, response) {
  structure(list(row_ids = row_ids, truth = truth, response = response),
    class = c("PredictionDataCount", "PredictionData"))
}

PredictionCount = R6Class("PredictionCount", inherit = Prediction,
  public = list(
    initialize = function(task = NULL, row_ids = task$row_ids, truth = task$truth(),
      response = NULL, check = TRUE) {
      pdata = new_prediction_data_count(row_ids, truth, response)
      if (check) pdata = check_prediction_data(pdata)
      self$task_type = "count"
      self$data = pdata
      self$predict_types = "response"
    }
  ),
  active = list(
    response = function() {
      if (is.null(self$data$response)) rep(NA_real_, length(self$data$row_ids)) else self$data$response
    }
  )
)

For the prediction data, a few S3 generics of {mlr3} have to be implemented: checking, filtering, and combining the prediction data, finding missing predictions, and converting it to a Prediction. In addition, create_empty_prediction_data() creates the prediction data when a learner predicts on a task without rows; it dispatches on the class of the task. Their implementations are straightforward, so we hide them below.

Implementation of the S3 methods 
as.data.table.PredictionCount = function(x, ...) {
  data.table(row_ids = x$row_ids, truth = x$truth, response = x$response)
}

check_prediction_data.PredictionDataCount = function(pdata, ...) {
  pdata$row_ids = checkmate::assert_integerish(pdata$row_ids, coerce = TRUE)
  pdata$response = checkmate::assert_numeric(unname(pdata$response), lower = 0,
    len = length(pdata$row_ids), null.ok = TRUE)
  pdata
}

is_missing_prediction_data.PredictionDataCount = function(pdata, ...) {
  pdata$row_ids[is.na(pdata$response)]
}

filter_prediction_data.PredictionDataCount = function(pdata, row_ids, ...) {
  keep = pdata$row_ids %in% row_ids
  pdata[c("row_ids", "truth", "response")] = lapply(pdata[c("row_ids", "truth", "response")],
    function(x) x[keep])
  pdata
}

c.PredictionDataCount = function(..., keep_duplicates = TRUE) {
  dots = list(...)
  pdata = lapply(c(row_ids = "row_ids", truth = "truth", response = "response"),
    function(nm) unlist(lapply(dots, `[[`, nm)))
  if (!keep_duplicates) {
    keep = !duplicated(pdata$row_ids, fromLast = TRUE)
    pdata = lapply(pdata, function(x) x[keep])
  }
  new_prediction_data_count(pdata$row_ids, pdata$truth, pdata$response)
}

as_prediction.PredictionDataCount = function(x, check = FALSE, ...) {
  PredictionCount$new(row_ids = x$row_ids, truth = x$truth, response = x$response, check = check)
}

create_empty_prediction_data.TaskCount = function(task, learner) {
  new_prediction_data_count(integer(), integer(), numeric())
}

Other S3 methods for tasks, such as head(), summary(), or partition(), are inherited from Task and need no dedicated implementation in this case. A package would usually also provide a converter as_task_count(), analogous to as_task_regr(), which we omit here. To see which methods a complete implementation of a task type should provide, look at an {mlr3} extension package that adds a task type, such as {mlr3survival}.

Because this code is run as an article here, we need to manually register the S3 methods. In a package, they are instead declared in the NAMESPACE file via S3method() (e.g., using roxygen’s @export tag).

Registration of the S3 methods 
for (generic in c("check_prediction_data", "is_missing_prediction_data",
  "filter_prediction_data", "c", "as_prediction")) {
  registerS3method(generic, "PredictionDataCount", get(paste0(generic, ".PredictionDataCount")))
}
registerS3method("as.data.table", "PredictionCount", as.data.table.PredictionCount)
for (generic in c("task_check_col_roles", "create_empty_prediction_data")) {
  registerS3method(generic, "TaskCount", get(paste0(generic, ".TaskCount")))
}

As the default measure, we use the (mean) Poisson deviance:

MeasureCountDeviance = R6Class("MeasureCountDeviance", inherit = Measure,
  public = list(
    initialize = function() {
      super$initialize(id = "count.deviance", task_type = "count",
        predict_type = "response", range = c(0, Inf), minimize = TRUE)
    }
  ),
  private = list(
    .score = function(prediction, ...) {
      y = prediction$truth
      mu = prediction$response
      2 * mean(ifelse(y == 0, 0, y * log(y / mu)) - (y - mu))
    }
  )
)
mlr_measures$add("count.deviance", MeasureCountDeviance)

The last line adds the measure to the dictionary mlr_measures under the key "count.deviance", so that it can be constructed via msr("count.deviance"). The default measure and the default loss of a task type, which we register below, are also specified by their keys and retrieved from these dictionaries.

Finally, we register the task type in mlr_reflections. Because our learner is quite similar to a regression learner and we want to keep things simple here, we reuse many of the settings from the regression task type. The package column names the package that provides the task type; "mlr3count" is a placeholder for the name of your extension package.

mlr_reflections$task_types = setkeyv(rbind(mlr_reflections$task_types, data.table(
  type = "count", package = "mlr3count", task = "TaskCount", learner = "Learner",
  prediction = "PredictionCount", prediction_data = "PredictionDataCount",
  measure = "MeasureCountDeviance"
), fill = TRUE), "type")
for (registry in c("task_col_roles", "task_properties", "learner_properties",
  "measure_properties")) {
  mlr_reflections[[registry]]$count = mlr_reflections[[registry]]$regr
}
mlr_reflections$learner_predict_types$count = list(response = "response")
mlr_reflections$default_measures$count = "count.deviance"

Supporting the Task Type in mlr3torch

{mlr3torch} has no separate learner classes per task type: all learners inherit from LearnerTorch, which takes the task_type as a construction argument. The task-type-specific behavior is defined by three S3 generics, which dispatch on the class of the task:

  • output_dim_for(): How many output units the network needs.
  • get_target_batchgetter(): How the target is converted to a tensor when loading the data.
  • encode_prediction(): How the output of the network (the torch tensor returned by its $forward() method) is converted into the data of a prediction.

For Poisson regression, the network has a single output unit, which we interpret as the log-rate.

output_dim_for.TaskCount = function(x, ...) 1L

get_target_batchgetter.TaskCount = function(task, ...) {
  function(data) torch_tensor(data[[1L]], dtype = torch_float32())$unsqueeze(2)
}

encode_prediction.TaskCount = function(task, network_output, predict_type, ...) {
  list(response = as.numeric(torch_exp(network_output)$cpu()))
}
Registration of the S3 methods 
registerS3method("output_dim_for", "TaskCount", output_dim_for.TaskCount)
registerS3method("get_target_batchgetter", "TaskCount", get_target_batchgetter.TaskCount)
registerS3method("encode_prediction", "TaskCount", encode_prediction.TaskCount)

Next, we need a loss for the new task type. Unlike the measure, which evaluates predictions in {mlr3} (e.g., in resampling or tuning), the loss is a differentiable function of the network output and the target tensor that is minimized during training. We add the Poisson negative log-likelihood to the mlr3torch_losses dictionary and declare that it can be used for the "count" task type.

mlr3torch_losses$add("poisson", function() {
  TorchLoss$new(torch_loss = nn_poisson_nll_loss, task_types = "count", id = "poisson",
    label = "Poisson NLL", man = "torch::nn_poisson_nll_loss")
})

Without further information, a learner for the new task type requires the loss to be passed explicitly:

LearnerTorchMLP$new(task_type = "count")
#> Error:
#> ! There is no default loss for task type 'count', pass the `loss` explicitly.

To make it the default loss for the task type, we register its id in mlr_reflections$torch$default_losses, which also holds the defaults for classification and regression.

mlr_reflections$torch$default_losses$count = "poisson"
mlr_reflections$torch$default_losses
#> $classif
#> [1] "cross_entropy"
#> 
#> $regr
#> [1] "mse"
#> 
#> $count
#> [1] "poisson"

Finally, we add the learners we want to offer for the new task type to the mlr_learners dictionary, here the multi-layer perceptron:

mlr_learners$add("count.mlp", function(...) LearnerTorchMLP$new(task_type = "count", ...))

This works for all learners whose architecture is agnostic to the task type, i.e., which only size their output layer via output_dim_for(). Some learners have task-specific parts, however. For example, TabM averages the predictions of its ensemble members differently for classification and regression in its private $.encode_prediction() method, so supporting a new task type requires overwriting this method.

Using the New Task Type

We simulate some count data, where the rate depends on two features. An actual extension package should also provide some example tasks, which are added to the mlr_tasks dictionary so that they can be constructed via tsk().

set.seed(42)
n = 1000
dat = data.table(x1 = runif(n, -1, 1), x2 = runif(n, -1, 1))
dat$y = rpois(n, exp(0.5 + dat$x1 - 0.5 * dat$x2))
task = TaskCount$new("sim_count", backend = dat, target = "y")
task
#> 
#> ── <TaskCount> (1000x3) ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> • Target: y
#> • Properties: -
#> • Features (2):
#>   • dbl (2): x1, x2

A non-integer target is rejected by task_check_col_roles():

TaskCount$new("invalid", backend = dat, target = "x1")
#> Error in `task_check_col_roles.TaskCount()`:
#> ! Target column 'x1' must be an integer column

The learner can now be constructed without specifying the loss, and the measure defaults to the Poisson deviance.

learner = lrn("count.mlp", epochs = 50, batch_size = 32, neurons = 16, opt.lr = 0.01)
learner$loss
#> <TorchLoss:poisson> Poisson NLL
#> * Generator: nn_poisson_nll_loss
#> * Parameters: list()
#> * Packages: torch,mlr3torch
#> * Task Types: count

Because the task type is registered with {mlr3}, everything just works, e.g. the learner can be resampled like any other learner:

rr = resample(task, learner, rsmp("holdout"))
rr$aggregate()
#> count.deviance 
#>       1.132842
head(as.data.table(rr$prediction()))
#>    row_ids truth response
#>      <int> <int>    <num>
#> 1:       6     4 2.422913
#> 2:      12     1 2.762603
#> 3:      14     2 1.368224
#> 4:      15     0 2.350587
#> 5:      21     2 2.940447
#> 6:      24     2 5.090517

Registration in a Package

In this article, we modified the registries mlr_reflections, mlr_measures, mlr3torch_losses, and mlr_learners directly. If you are working on a package, this should be done in the .onLoad() hook instead, see {mlr3survival}’s .onLoad() implementation for an example. This requires the package whose registries are extended to be in Imports. If it is only in Suggests, e.g., to make {mlr3torch} an optional dependency, it may not be loaded yet when your package is loaded, so the registrations have to be done in a callback that runs once it is loaded, which can be registered via mlr3misc::register_namespace_callback().
